vocab.context: The safe default. Use it with anyone you're not close to. 'Tanaka-san' works for a boss, a stranger, or a character you just met in episode one.

meanings.en: suffix for boys / younger males / informal respect
meanings.pt-BR: sufixo para garotos / homens mais jovens

vocab.context: Added to a boy's name by someone older or in authority. Teachers use it for male students. 'Deku-kun' — affectionate from Uraraka, formal from teachers.
Warmth in a syllable. Used for girls, small children, pets, and close friends regardless of gender. 'Nami-chan', 'Pikachu-chan'. Also signals cuteness-as-personality.

One of the most loaded words in anime. The idol you look up to — Oikawa to Kageyama in Haikyuu, Makoto to Haruka in Free!. When a kouhai finally says 'senpai' with their whole chest, something has shifted.
Anyone who teaches or masters a craft. Kakashi-sensei, Iruka-sensei. Also used for doctors and manga artists. The respect embedded in one word.
Reserved for nobility, gods, and characters with overwhelming power or status. 'Vegeta-sama'. 'Ainz-sama'. If someone bows their head when they say your name, this is why.

The honorific of the samurai age. More equal than 様 — used even to peers of high standing. 'Himura-dono' from Rurouni Kenshin. If you're watching a period drama and everyone speaks with formality, this is everywhere.

meanings.pt-BR: mestre / sensei de artes marciais / mentor

vocab.context: The master who trains you in a craft or fighting style. More intimate and specific than 先生. 'Jiraiya-shishou' — your teacher by blood-and-sweat bond.

meanings.en: extremely cute / baby-talk diminutive of ちゃん
meanings.pt-BR: fofíssimo / diminutivo babão de ちゃん
meanings.es: muy adorable / diminutivo infantil de ちゃん

vocab.context: ちゃん with the dial turned to max cute. Used in moe anime, fan communities, and mascot characters. 'Mikuru-tan'. If you're being called this, you're adorable.
Almost exclusively written. You'll see it in news broadcasts and official documents inside anime. If a character reads aloud from a paper, this will be there.

meanings.en: underclassman / junior / someone below you in seniority
meanings.es: novato / junior / alguien menor en antigüedad

vocab.context: The counterpart to 先輩. The younger student who looks up to you. Romance anime often centers on the senpai-kouhai dynamic — the kouhai who caught the senpai's eye.
Attached to nouns to make them polite. 'O-namae' (your name), 'o-cha' (tea), 'o-kane' (money). Female characters and formal speech use it liberally.

meanings.en: older brother / used to address young male strangers
meanings.pt-BR: irmão mais velho / forma de chamar jovens desconhecidos
meanings.es: hermano mayor / forma de dirigirse a jóvenes desconocidos

vocab.context: Used for actual older brothers and to address unfamiliar young men warmly. Mei uses it for Totoro without a second thought. Shopkeepers, children, and passersby use it as a casual open address.

meanings.en: older sister / used to address young female strangers
meanings.pt-BR: irmã mais velha / forma de chamar jovens desconhecidas
meanings.es: hermana mayor / forma de dirigirse a jóvenes desconocidas

vocab.context: The sister-side counterpart to onii-san. Said by children to adult women in shops, in parks, on trains. A gentle address that keeps the social distance warm rather than formal.

meanings.en: calling someone by name with no suffix (intimacy marker)

vocab.context: Dropping a suffix is never accidental. It can mean deep intimacy (the confession arc moment) or contempt (a villain addressing the hero without respect). Same word, opposite meanings — the gap between them is everything.
